paper: U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation
dataset: Evaluated on microscopy datasets (not liver segmentation): ISBI 2012 EM segmentation challenge (30 images of 512x512 pixels, serial section transmission electron microscopy) and ISBI Cell Tracking Challenge 2015 datasets ('PhC-U373' with 35 phase contrast images and 'DIC-HeLa' with 20 differential interference contrast microscopy images).
method: A symmetric encoder-decoder fully convolutional network that connects contracting contextual feature maps to an expansive localization path via skip connections, trained end-to-end with extensive random elastic deformations and a touching-boundary weighted loss.
metric: Warping error, Rand error, Pixel error, and Intersection over Union (IOU)
result: Achieved state-of-the-art warping error of 0.000353 and rand error of 0.0382 on the ISBI EM stack challenge, and outranked competitors on the ISBI Cell Tracking Challenge with an average IOU of 0.9203 (92.0%) on PhC-U373 and 0.7756 (77.5%) on DIC-HeLa.
limitation: The paper focuses entirely on 2D microscopy cell and membrane segmentation rather than organ or liver segmentation; additionally, unpadded convolutions reduce output resolution relative to the input, requiring mirroring extrapolation and an overlap-tile strategy to process larger images.

paper: Attention U-Net: Learning Where to Look for the Pancreas
dataset: Evaluated on CT-150 (150 3D abdominal CT scans) and NIH-TCIA Pancreas-CT / CT-82 (82 contrast-enhanced 3D CT scans), both resampled to 2.0 mm isotropic resolution. Note: The paper is focused on pancreas segmentation and does not report liver segmentation evaluation results.
method: Integrates additive soft attention gates into U-Net skip connections to filter feature activations using contextual gating signals from coarser scales, eliminating the need for cascaded external localization networks.
metric: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Surface-to-Surface Distance (S2S in mm), Precision, Recall
result: On CT-150 (120 train / 30 test), Attention U-Net achieved a pancreas DSC of 0.840 +/- 0.087 (vs. 0.814 +/- 0.116 for standard U-Net), pancreas S2S of 1.920 +/- 1.284 mm, spleen DSC of 0.965 +/- 0.013, and kidney DSC of 0.964 +/- 0.016; on TCIA CT-82 after fine-tuning, it achieved a pancreas DSC of 0.831 +/- 0.038 (and 81.48 +/- 6.23% in 5-fold cross-validation).
limitation: The study does not evaluate or report results for liver segmentation; furthermore, scans had to be downsampled to 2.0 mm isotropic resolution due to GPU memory constraints, and incorporating residual connections around attention gate blocks did not provide significant performance gains.

paper: UNet++: A Nested U-Net Architecture for Medical Image Segmentation
dataset: The paper is not primarily about liver segmentation, but evaluates across four medical segmentation datasets: liver CT (331 images, 512x512, MICCAI 2018 LiTS Challenge), cell nuclei microscopy (670 images, 96x96, Data Science Bowl 2018), colon polyp RGB video (7,379 images, 224x224, ASU-Mayo), and lung nodule CT (1,012 images, 64x64x64, LIDC-IDRI).
method: UNet++ redesigns skip pathways by connecting encoder and decoder sub-networks through a series of nested, dense convolutional blocks combined with deep supervision to reduce the semantic gap between feature maps prior to fusion.
result: On the liver dataset, UNet++ with deep supervision (DS) achieved 82.90% IoU (and 79.70% without DS), outperforming standard U-Net (76.62%) and Wide U-Net (76.58%); across all four datasets, UNet++ with DS achieved an average IoU gain of 3.9 and 3.4 points over U-Net and Wide U-Net, respectively.
limitation: The benefits of deep supervision vary across tasks (it vanished for cell nuclei and colon polyps), and while pruning UNet++ at inference time reduces latency (e.g., L3 reduces inference time by 32.2%), more aggressive pruning causes significant accuracy degradation.

paper: nnU-Net: Self-adapting Framework for U-Net-Based Medical Image Segmentation
dataset: Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Phase 1 tasks (7 datasets across CT and MRI modalities: BrainTumour, Heart, Liver CT, Hippocampus, Prostate, Lung CT, Pancreas CT; paper is not primarily about liver segmentation but a general challenge benchmark)
model: nnU-Net (2D U-Net, 3D U-Net, and U-Net Cascade, plus ensembles)
method: A self-adapting segmentation framework based on standard U-Nets that automatically configures network topology, preprocessing, training, inference, and post-processing according to dataset geometry and hardware constraints without manual intervention.
result: On the MSD Phase 1 test set, nnU-Net achieved Dice scores of 95.24 (liver) and 73.71 (tumor) on the Liver CT task using an ensemble of 3D U-Net + 3D U-Net Cascade (cross-validation Dice: 95.43 and 61.82), attaining the highest leaderboard Dice scores across all Phase 1 tasks and classes except BrainTumour class 1.
limitation: The paper is not primarily focused on liver segmentation; practically, training three separate models per dataset to select the best is computationally intensive, and many specific design choices (such as Leaky ReLU or specific augmentation parameters) were not validated via ablation studies.

dataset: Liver Tumor Segmentation Benchmark (LiTS) dataset consisting of 201 contrast-enhanced abdominal CT volumes (131 training and 70 unseen test scans) acquired from seven international clinical centers.
model: Benchmark evaluating 75 submitted algorithms, dominated by 2D, 2.5D, and 3D U-Net variants (e.g., cascaded ResNet/U-Nets, H-DenseUNet, and 3D nnU-Net).
method: A multi-center benchmarking challenge evaluating automated multi-stage, cascaded, and self-configuring deep convolutional neural network approaches for liver segmentation, liver tumor segmentation, and lesion detection.
metric: Dice score (per case), Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASD in mm), Relative Volume Difference (RVD), Lesion-wise Precision, Recall, and F1 score (stratified into small <10 mm, medium 10–20 mm, and large >20 mm).
result: For liver segmentation, the best method achieved a Dice of 0.963 (ASD: 1.104 mm). For liver tumor segmentation, winning Dice scores progressed from 0.674 (ISBI 2017) to 0.702 (MICCAI 2017) and 0.739 (MICCAI 2018 by F. Isensee et al., ASD: 0.903 mm). In tumor detection, best overall lesion recall reached 0.554, but small lesion (<10 mm) detection remained very challenging with top F1 scores of only 0.10–0.24.
limitation: Initial annotations were performed slice-wise by only one rater per center, introducing inter-rater variability and potential label noise; algorithms performed poorly on small lesions (<10 mm) and scans with low liver-to-lesion contrast (<20 HU); generalizability to unseen centers was not evaluated; and overlap-based top performers often exhibited high false-positive rates in tumor detection.
